title-group.article-title: Hypoxia Preserves Chromatin Integrity and Delays Cellular Senescence through Epigenetic Regulation

abstract.p: Hypoxia is a physiologically relevant microenvironment in both normal and diseased tissues and has emerged as a potent modulator of cellular senescence and organismal longevity. This review synthesizes evidence that hypoxia delays senescence across diverse experimental systems and species, and highlights mechanisms by which hypoxia rewires chromatin states during senescence-associated transitions. We focus on oxygen- and α-ketoglutarate–dependent epigenetic regulators, particularly histone lysine demethylases, whose catalytic activities are limited under hypoxia. Consequently, histone methylation increases and higher-order chromatin organization is stabilized. Using oncogene-induced senescence as an experimentally tractable framework, we discuss recent findings showing that hypoxia suppresses senescence-associated histone clipping, preserves nuclear lamina integrity, and restrains large-scale heterochromatin reorganization while leaving canonical cell-cycle arrest largely intact. We further consider emerging links among DNA damage, epigenetic instability, and aging phenotypes, and propose that senescence can be viewed as a breakdown of coordinated epigenetic homeostasis. By integrating these concepts, we position hypoxia and hypoxia-mimetic interventions as promising strategies to modulate aging-associated cellular states and to explore therapeutic opportunities in age-related pathologies.

sec.title: HYPOXIA AS A MODULATOR OF CELLULAR SENESCENCE AND LONGEVITY
Physiological and pathological contexts of hypoxia
sec.p: Oxygen concentration in peripheral tissues varies widely, ranging from approximately 0.1% to 8%, depending on the balance between vascular oxygen supply and cellular oxygen consumption. Profoundly hypoxic regions (0.1-1% O₂) are commonly observed in solid tumors as well as in specialized stem cell niches, indicating that hypoxia is not merely a pathological condition but also a physiologically relevant microenvironment (Mohyeldin et al., 2010; Sullivan et al., 2008). Within these contexts, hypoxia profoundly influences cellular fate decisions. In tumors hypoxic cancer cells frequently acquire resistance to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, while stem cells exposed to low oxygen resist differentiation and preferentially maintain stemness. Hypoxia supports a microenvironmental niche that favors quiescent survival under metabolic stress rather than directly inducing therapy-related dormancy. In this context, hypoxia-associated factors such as TGFβ2 and p27 contribute to the maintenance of quiescent survival within the hypoxic niche (Butturini et al., 2019). Although non-proliferative, these dormant cells remain viable after treatment and can persist for extended periods, ultimately serving as a reservoir for tumor recurrence. Thus, hypoxia not only compromises immediate therapeutic efficacy but also shapes long-term cellular trajectories that underlie cancer persistence and relapse (Triana-Martinez et al., 2020).

sec.title: Hypoxia delays senescence and extends lifespan
sec.p: Beyond cancer biology, hypoxic conditions have long been associated with delayed cellular senescence and lifespan extension across diverse organisms. When cultured under physiological oxygen levels (approximately 3%), mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) fail to undergo replicative senescence, whereas cells maintained under atmospheric oxygen (20-21%) accumulate substantially more DNA damage (Ezzati et al., 2012; Krivoruchko and Storey, 2010; Lutz et al., 2003; Otero-Albiol and Carnero, 2021; Parrinello et al., 2003; Rogers et al., 2023). Reduced oxygen tension similarly extends replicative lifespan in primary human lung fibroblast, primary human mesenchymal stem cell, and human natural killer cells (Leontieva et al., 2012; Lim et al., 2021; Tsai et al., 2011). The anti-senescent effects of hypoxia are conserved across species. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, hypoxia induced by limited aeration extends chronological lifespan, with even brief hypoxic exposure during early growth conferring long-term survival benefits (Bonawitz et al., 2007). In Caenorhabditis elegans, exposure to 0.5% oxygen during the L4 larval stage increases median lifespan in a manner dependent on hypoxia-responsive transcription (Leiser et al., 2013; Rogers and Mootha, 2025). The naked mole rat (Heterocephalus glaber), which inhabits crowded subterranean burrows with estimated oxygen levels of approximately 6%, exhibits an exceptionally long lifespan exceeding 30 years—nearly tenfold longer than that of common laboratory rats (Pamenter, 2022). Likewise, human populations residing at high altitudes, such as those in Tibetan and Andean regions where ambient oxygen levels of approximately 11%, display increased longevity (Burtscher et al., 2025; Ezzati et al., 2012; Li et al., 2017; Wuren et al., 2014).

Direct experimental evidence that oxygen restriction, analogous to dietary restriction, can modulate mammalian aging comes from studies using the Ercc1Δ/− mouse model of accelerated aging (Rogers et al., 2023; Weeda et al., 1997). These mice harbor defects in nucleotide excision repair, leading to rapid accumulation of DNA damage, early onset of senescence-associated phenotypes, and a markedly shortened lifespan (Cagan et al., 2022; Lopez-Otin et al., 2013). Remarkably, exposure to continuous hypoxia (11% oxygen) beginning at 4 weeks of age extends lifespan by approximately 50% and delays neurological decline. Importantly, hypoxia does not significantly alter food intake or canonical markers of DNA damage and senescence, suggesting that oxygen restriction does not simply compensate for defective DNA repair but instead acts through downstream or parallel mechanisms (Rogers et al., 2023).

sec.title: O₂-SENSING EPIGENETIC REGULATORS UNDER HYPOXIA
sec.p: Hypoxia influences a broad spectrum of cellular processes, including angiogenesis, erythropoiesis, glycolysis, tumor invasion, and metastasis, while simultaneously repressing differentiation, tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle activity, and cellular senescence (Lee et al., 2020; Semenza, 2012; Wicks and Semenza, 2022). Many of these hypoxia-driven responses are mediated by oxygen-sensitive regulators whose activities are directly constrained by oxygen availability. These include hypoxia-inducible transcription factors (HIFs) as well as a broader class of oxygen- and α-ketoglutarate (α-KG)–dependent dioxygenases that regulate histone, DNA, and RNA methylation (Fig. 1) (Agger et al., 2007; Chang et al., 2019; Ivan et al., 2001; Jaakkola et al., 2001; Seward et al., 2007; Shen et al., 2014; Shi and Whetstine, 2007; Whetstine et al., 2006; Wu et al., 2017).

sec.title: Canonical oxygen sensing through HIF signaling
sec.p: The best-characterized oxygen-sensing pathway involves activation of hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF), a heterodimeric transcription factor composed of an oxygen-sensitive α subunit (HIF-1α or HIF-2α/EPAS1) and a constitutively expressed β subunit (HIF-1β/ARNT) (Ivan et al., 2001; Semenza, 2001; Wang et al., 1995). Under normoxic conditions, HIF-α is hydroxylated at conserved proline residues by prolyl hydroxylase domain proteins (PHDs), which require molecular oxygen and α-ketoglutarate (α-KG) as co-substrates. Hydroxylated HIF-α is recognized by the von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) E3 ubiquitin ligase and targeted for proteasomal degradation (Jaakkola et al., 2001). Hypoxia suppresses this hydroxylation, allowing HIF-α stabilization, heterodimerization with ARNT, and binding to hypoxia-responsive elements across hundreds of target genes (Fig. 2) (Lee et al., 2017).

HIF-α transcriptional activity is further regulated by asparagine hydroxylation mediated by factor inhibiting HIF (FIH), another oxygen- and α-KG–dependent dioxygenase (Mahon et al., 2001). Notably, FIH contains a Jumonji C (JmjC) domain, a motif later recognized as a defining feature of a large family of histone lysine demethylases. This shared catalytic architecture provided an early conceptual link between oxygen sensing and epigenetic regulation (Fig. 3) (Black et al., 2012).

sec.title: Oxygen-dependent histone demethylases as epigenetic sensors
sec.p: Beyond HIF regulation, hypoxia directly impacts chromatin and epigenetic regulation through inhibition of oxygen-dependent demethylases. JmjC-domain–containing histone lysine demethylases (KDMs), as well as related dioxygenases that act on DNA (TET family) and RNA (ALKBH/FTO family), require molecular oxygen and α-KG for catalytic activity (Fig. 1, 3A, 3B) (Black et al., 2012; Shen et al., 2014). Although these enzymes share common co-substrates, their kinetic parameters, — particularly the Km values for oxygen and α-KG— differ substantially, rendering individual demethylases differentially sensitive to reduced oxygen availability (Table 1) (Chang et al., 2019; Diehl and Muir, 2020; Kooistra and Helin, 2012). To date, more than 20 JmjC-domain–containing KDMs have been identified, each with distinct substrate specificities and oxygen sensitivities. Under severe hypoxic conditions (typically <0.5% O₂), global levels of histone methylation increase, consistent with selective inhibition of oxygen-sensitive histone demethylase activities (Krieg et al., 2010; Laukka et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2013, 2017; Shi et al., 2004).

sec.title: Metabolic control of epigenetic regulation under hypoxia
sec.p: Histone modifications are dynamically regulated by three classes of proteins : writers, which deposit covalent marks; erasers, which remove them; and readers, which recognize modified histones and recruit transcriptional, replicative, repair or structural complexes (Hyun et al., 2017). Importantly, both writers and erasers depend on metabolic intermediates—such as S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), α-KG, reducing cofactors, and molecular oxygen—placing chromatin regulation at the intersection of metabolism and oxygen sensing (Chang et al., 2019; Diehl and Muir, 2020; Schvartzman et al., 2018). Hypoxia profoundly rewires cellular metabolism by promoting glycolysis and suppressing mitochondrial oxidative metabolism. This shift is driven by HIF-dependent induction of glycolytic enzymes and pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK), which inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase and limits acetyl-CoA production (Bell et al., 2007; Hamanaka et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2006). Hypoxia also enhances mitophagy via induction of BNIP3 and BNIP3L, facilitating the selective removal of damaged mitochondria (Bellot et al., 2009). Chronic hypoxia can reduce intracellular α-KG levels when glutamine- and glutamate-derived anaplerotic inputs are limited, and promotes the accumulation of L-2-hydroxyglutarate (L-2HG), an oncometabolite that competitively inhibits α-KG–dependent dioxygenases, including KDMs (Fig. 4) (Chang et al., 2019; Dang et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2011). By simultaneously rewiring metabolism and constraining oxygen-dependent epigenetic erasers, hypoxia promotes a hypermethylated chromatin landscape (Chowdhury et al., 2011; Intlekofer et al., 2015; Oldham et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2011).

sec.title: Transcriptional noise and loss of epigenetic constraint
sec.p: Cellular senescence represents a stable cellular state characterized by irreversible cell-cycle arrest and progressive loss of cellular identity (Baker and Sedivy, 2013; Di Micco et al., 2006; Gorgoulis et al., 2019; Hernandez-Segura et al., 2018; Miwa et al., 2022; Moiseeva et al., 2009; Sen et al., 2016; Sun et al., 2016; Takasugi et al., 2023). Cellular identity is maintained by cell type–specific transcriptional programs, whose fidelity depends critically on epigenetic mechanisms that constrain chromatin accessibility and suppress inappropriate gene expression (Fig. 5). Single-cell transcriptomic analyses of young and aged tissues have revealed that aging is accompanied by a marked increase in transcriptional variability at the level of individual cells (Enge et al., 2017; Goodell and Rando, 2015; Hong et al., 2023; Jia et al., 2023; Levy et al., 2020; Swisa et al., 2017; Xin et al., 2016). Landmark studies, including analyses of human pancreatic islet cells, demonstrated that aged cells exhibit elevated transcriptional noise and evidence of fate drift, indicating that aging proceeds as a stochastic and heterogeneous process rather than a uniform genetic program (Enge et al., 2017). Similar increases in transcriptional variability have also been reported across diverse tissues (Goodell and Rando, 2015; Hong et al., 2023)

At a mechanistic level, chromatin structure dictates the accessibility of promoters and regulatory elements, thereby shaping transcriptional output. (Klemm et al., 2019; Pollex et al., 2024; Uyehara and Apostolou, 2023). Combinatorial post-translational modifications of histones specify chromatin states and precisely constrain transcriptional programs. (Table 2) (Jenuwein and Allis, 2001; Millan-Zambrano et al., 2022; Su and Denu, 2016; Taverna et al., 2007; Tessarz et al., 2014). Based on the diversity of histone modifications reported in the literature (Millan-Zambrano et al., 2022), epigenetic constraints are finely tuned by histone codes, which can theoretically generate up to ~1×10174 distinct combinatorial states on a single histone octamer, together with their corresponding reader proteins (Table 2).

During aging, the integrity of these histone code–based epigenetic constraints progressively weakens. As a consequence, increased transcriptional noise is not merely the result of random transcriptional errors but reflects an entropic drift arising from stochastic disorganization of histone modification patterns that collectively constitute the histone code across the genome (Fig. 5). A central unresolved question is why chromatin structure becomes progressively destabilized during aging, and whether specific environmental conditions—such as hypoxia—can reinforce epigenetic constraints to suppress transcriptional noise and stabilize chromatin architecture.

sec.title: Age-associated DNA methylation remodeling
sec.p: In addition to transcriptional noise, aging is accompanied by highly reproducible changes in DNA methylation. Statistical analyses have identified specific CpG sites whose methylation status correlates strongly with chronological age, forming the basis of DNA methylation–based epigenetic clocks (Horvath, 2013; Maierhofer et al., 2017; Petkovich et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017). Although global DNA methylation levels generally decline with age, a defined subset of CpG sites consistently undergoes hyper- or hypomethylation across tissues and species. The methylation patterns at these age-associated CpG sites enable accurate prediction of biological age, which often diverges from chronological age (Unnikrishnan et al., 2019). Defining how such ordered epigenetic patterns emerge and are maintained during aging remains a central challenge in aging biology.

sec.title: Oncogene-induced senescence and senescence-associated heterochromatin foci
sec.p: Oncogene-induced senescence (OIS), triggered by enforced activation of oncogenes such as Ras, Raf, or Myc in primary cells, induces a rapid and stable senescent state through activation of the p53 and Rb tumor suppressor pathways (Baker and Sedivy, 2013; Di Micco et al., 2006). OIS is widely recognized as an intrinsic tumor-suppressive mechanism that constrains early tumorigenic progression (Wang et al., 2024). Although both replicative senescence and OIS culminate in irreversible cell-cycle arrest, they differ markedly in their effects on higher-order chromatin organization (Falk et al., 2019; Sen et al., 2016; Solovei et al., 2013). A defining cytological feature of OIS is large-scale spatial reorganization of heterochromatin. In proliferating cells, heterochromatin is predominantly tethered to the nuclear periphery through interactions between lamins, HP1, and H3K9me3, whereas OIS cells frequently display redistribution of heterochromatic domains toward the nuclear interior (Fig. 5) (Chang et al., 2025). This reorganization, termed senescence-associated heterochromatin foci (SAHF), represents a striking and reproducible manifestation of senescence-associated chromatin remodeling.

Mechanistically, during OIS, reductions in both lamin B1 and H3K9me3 levels weaken lamina–heterochromatin interactions, facilitating detachment from the nuclear periphery (Sadaie et al., 2013). Polymer modeling and quantitative imaging analyses indicate that lamina detachment alone is insufficient to explain SAHF formation (Chiang et al., 2019; Sati et al., 2020). Instead, homotypic interactions among heterochromatic regions promote phase separation from euchromatin, enabling the emergence of discrete SAHF within the nuclear interior (Belaghzal et al., 2021; Falk et al., 2019). In addition to HP1–H3K9me3 interactions, other chromatin-associated factors, including H3K27me3-marked regions, HMGB family proteins, and DNMT1, contribute to intranuclear segregation of heterochromatin during OIS (Zirkel et al., 2018).

Population-based Hi-C studies, together with single-cell transcriptomic and imaging analyses, suggest that senescent cell populations exhibit substantial heterogeneity in chromatin organization, although direct single-cell Hi-C evidence in senescence remains limited. (Shaban and Gasser, 2025; Zirkel et al., 2018). Chromatin loops and compartmental segregation patterns vary substantially within senescent populations, indicating that oncogene-induced senescence is associated with a spectrum of chromatin states rather than a uniform architectural outcome. Consequently, senescence-associated chromatin reorganization, including SAHF, differentially alters nuclear architecture across individual cells, increasing the diversity of transcriptional states accessible to each cell and giving rise to the cell-to-cell heterogeneity and transcriptional variability observed during OIS (Fig. 5) (Olan et al., 2023).

Beyond changes in histone modifications and nuclear architecture, OIS is also associated with proteolytic remodeling of chromatin (Chang et al., 2025). The lysosomal protease cathepsin L has been reported to translocate to the nucleus during senescence, where it cleaves histone N-terminal tails. This proteolytic processing introduces an additional layer of chromatin regulation that may further influence chromatin stability and higher-order organization during OIS (Table 2) (Duncan, 2025).

sec.title: DNA damage, epigenetic disruption, and convergent senescence states
sec.p: Progeroid syndromes caused by inherited defects in diverse cellular systems including the nuclear lamina, mitochondrial function, and DNA repair pathways, converge on premature senescence and chromatin disorganization. Notably, diverse acquired cellular stresses can drive cells toward a remarkably similar senescence-associated state, underscoring convergence at the level of cellular state rather than a single linear initiating mechanism (Rieckher et al., 2021; Soto-Palma et al., 2022). Recently, in vivo evidence further supports the idea that aging phenotypes can arise from epigenetic disruption triggered by DNA damage. Yang and colleagues demonstrated that inducible DNA double-strand breaks—referred to by the authors as ICE (Inducible Changes to the Epigenome)—are sufficient to accelerate biological aging in mice in a model designed to induce controlled DNA breaks with minimal detectable mutagenesis (Teefy and Benayoun, 2023; Yang et al., 2023b). This model provides compelling evidence that DNA double-strand breaks that primarily perturb the epigenome, even without overt cytotoxicity or loss of cellular function, can promote aging-associated phenotypes. Together, these findings support a state-centric model in which diverse insults converge on aging-associated phenotypes through perturbation of epigenetic constraints. How such perturbations are manifested at the level of epigenetic heterogeneity across individual cells remains to be determined.

Unlike transcriptional regulation, which can be readily interrogated at defined genomic elements such as promoters and enhancers (Klemm et al., 2019), chromatin regulation in the context of DNA damage lacks fixed genomic coordinates. DNA lesions are transient, heterogeneous, and asynchronous across cell populations, rendering damage-associated histone modification signals difficult to capture using conventional genome-wide approaches such as ChIP-seq. Consequently, while histone modifications have been extensively mapped in transcriptional contexts, their roles in DNA repair and genome maintenance remain less systematically characterized (Soto-Palma et al., 2022). This gap hinders efforts to integrate DNA damage–associated chromatin regulation into unified models of epigenetic aging and senescence. Nevertheless, despite the absence of system-level datasets, multiple lines of evidence indicate that histone lysine demethylases (KDMs) targeting H3K4, H3K36, H3K9, and H3K27 participate directly in DNA damage responses (Gong and Miller, 2019). Because these enzymes are oxygen- and α-KG–dependent, hypoxic conditions have the potential to modulate DNA repair–associated chromatin states by constraining KDM activity.

sec.title: HYPOXIA PRESERVES CHROMATIN INTEGRITY DURING OIS
sec.p: Oncogene-induced senescence (OIS) provides a powerful and experimentally tractable model for investigating histone methylation, nuclear lamina integrity, and higher-order chromatin organization during senescence. Induction of oncogenes for only 4-6 days is sufficient to elicit a robust senescent state, accompanied by canonical senescence markers, including SA-β-gal activity, senescence-associated secretory phenotypes (SASP), and induction of p16INK4a and p21CIP1. Importantly, OIS uniquely allows direct visualization of SAHF by microscopy, enabling direct assessment of large-scale chromatin reorganization during senescence onset (Chang et al., 2025).

Using top-down proteomic analyses, Chang et al. (2025) identified selective proteolytic cleavage of histones H3, H2B, and H4 during OIS, occurring at H3 A21/T22, H2B T19/K20, and H4 G11/K12, respectively (Table 2). In contrast, histone H2A remained intact, indicating a histone-specific cleavage process. These cleavage events were mediated by the lysosomal protease cathepsin L, revealing an additional and previously underappreciated layer of chromatin remodeling associated with senescence (Chang et al., 2025). The causal relationships among histone clipping, chromatin reorganization, and nuclear architecture during OIS have yet to be fully resolved. Notably, hypoxia suppresses histone clipping, SAHF formation, and nuclear lamina destabilization while preserving Rb and p53 pathway activity downstream of oncogene activation. Thus, hypoxia does not prevent OIS by blocking oncogene-induced cell-cycle arrest, but instead modulates chromatin-associated events that occur subsequent to senescence initiation.

Pharmacological inhibition of histone lysine demethylases (KDMs) using the pan-KDM inhibitor JIB-04 effectively blocks histone clipping, indicating that histone methylation status critically influences susceptibility to proteolytic processing. In vitro competitive enzyme kinetic assays further demonstrated that methylation at H3K23 and H3K18—residues flanking the cleavage site—reduces the susceptibility of histone H3 to cathepsin L, suggesting that methylation of cleavage-proximal residues directly protects histones from irreversible cleavage. One plausible mechanism is that H3K18/23 trimethylation facilitates the recruitment of reader proteins that shield histone H3 from cathepsin L access.

However, KDM inhibition alone is insufficient to prevent SAHF formation. While KDM inhibition does not prevent the OIS-associated reduction of nuclear lamins, hypoxia robustly preserves lamin integrity. These observations indicate that hypoxia exerts broader protective effects on nuclear architecture that extend beyond the maintenance of histone methylation. The nuclear envelope is mechanically supported by coordinated interactions among heterochromatin, nuclear lamina components, and the actin cytoskeleton (Ungricht and Kutay, 2017). Hypoxia is associated with enhanced perinuclear actin organization, suggesting that hypoxic potentiation of the cytoskeleton may contribute to the mechanical support and structural stability of nuclear architecture during senescence, although the mechanistic basis of this effect has yet to be fully elucidated (Stephens and Miroshnikova, 2024).

Histone clipping has been observed across diverse species and cellular contexts, including mouse intestinal villi, human monocytes, yeast sporulation, and neuronal differentiation of stem cells (Chang et al., 2025; Cheung et al., 2021; Duarte et al., 2014; Duncan, 2025; Duncan et al., 2008; Ferrari et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2023a) (Table 2). This rare but irreversible post-translational modification is typically associated with terminal differentiation or stable cell fate transitions, including oncogene-induced senescence (Corpet et al., 2014; O’Sullivan et al., 2010; Tagami et al., 2004). Unless counteracted by de novo histone synthesis, histone clipping represents a permanent alteration of chromatin structure, underscoring its potential significance in directing long-term cellular outcomes. Consistent with this notion, ChIP-seq analysis using an H3cs1 (H3 cleaved site 1)-specific antibody revealed enrichment of cleaved H3 at open chromatin regions and transcription start sites (TSS) of active genes in human monocytes (Cheung et al., 2021). Similarly, ATAC-seq analysis of OIS cells demonstrated preferential histone clipping within accessible euchromatin, rather than within condensed heterochromatin such as lamina-associated domains (LADs) (Chang et al., 2025). These findings raise the possibility that histone clipping occurs downstream of chromatin opening, rather than serving as its initiating event.

Together, these findings suggest that histone clipping selectively targets transcriptionally permissive chromatin and introduces irreversible chromatin alterations that constrain subsequent transcriptional plasticity whereas hypoxia limits this process by reinforcing histone methylation and overall chromatin stability, thereby preserving a chromatin state that remains amenable to dynamic histone modification in response to diverse signals.

Collectively, these observations indicate that hypoxia suppresses aging and senescence not through a single dominant pathway, but by reshaping cellular environments toward low-damage, low-entropy states. Rather than reversing senescence programs, hypoxia limits the propagation of senescence-associated chromatin instability by modulating metabolism, redox balance, histone modification, and nuclear architecture. Through these coordinated effects, hypoxia slows the transition from transient stress responses to stable senescence-associated cellular states.

sec.title: HYPOXIC THERAPEUTICS
sec.p: Ischemia, defined by an interruption of blood supply rather than reduced oxygen availability per se, has long been recognized as a potent trigger of cell death. In contrast, accumulating evidence that hypoxia can delay senescence and extend lifespan raises the possibility that hypoxia, or hypoxia-mimetic strategies, may be harnessed to modulate aging-associated cellular states and mitochondrial diseases in therapeutic contexts (Rogers and Mootha, 2025). Biochemical characterization of oxygen-sensing enzymes, including prolyl hydroxylase domain protein 2 (PHD2), factor inhibiting HIF-1 (FIH-1), KDM4 family histone demethylases (H3K9me3 demethylases), KDM5, and TET1, revealed Km values in the range of 30 to 250 µM, corresponding to oxygen concentrations near physiological levels in peripheral tissues (Table 1) (Chang et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2017; Mohyeldin et al., 2010). These findings suggest that basal levels of HIF-α activity and the methylated histones marks such as H3K9me3 are likely higher in vivo at around 3% oxygen than in standard cell culture conditions maintained at 20% oxygen. In the setting of mitochondrial electron transport chain dysfunction, “unused” oxygen may accumulate to levels exceeding the Km values of oxygen-dependent enzymes. This can result in aberrant activation of PHDs, FIH, and KDMs, thereby suppressing HIF signaling and reducing levels of methylated histones and DNA. This observation raises the intriguing possibility that chronic continuous hypoxia (CCH) may restore the basal tone of hypoxia-sensing and epigenetic regulatory pathways in inherited or acquired mitochondrial disorders that are frequently observed in aged individuals (Fig. 3) (Table 1).

Consistent with this concept, preclinical studies have demonstrated that CCH at 10-11% oxygen confers substantial benefit in mouse models of mitochondrial disease, including Leigh syndrome (LS) (Jain et al., 2016) and Friedreich’s ataxia (Rogers and Mootha, 2025) all of which share impaired mitochondrial respiration. Paradoxically, CCH has also shown protective effects in mouse models of myocardial infarction and ischemic stroke (Nakada et al., 2017; Rogers and Mootha, 2025) echoing long-standing clinical observations of hypoxic preconditioning in ischemia–reperfusion injury, although the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood.

sec.title: Hypoxic conditioning: opportunities and limitations
sec.p: Athletic training strategies such as “live high altitude (low-oxygen conditions), train low altitude,” in which individuals sleep in hypoxic tents with nitrogen-diluted air, are well established and commercially available (Wilber, 2007). However, multiple barriers complicate clinical translation of CCH effects. First, patients exhibit far greater interindividual variability in oxygen metabolism. Second, the timing and duration of hypoxic exposure is critical. Third, acute and chronic risks including pulmonary and cerebral edema must be carefully considered. Fourth, humans possess robust homeostatic mechanisms that defend brain oxygenation, including hyperventilation, tachycardia, and erythropoiesis. Finally, non-invasive and accurate measurement of tissue oxygenation in organs such as the brain remains a major technical hurdle.

sec.title: Hypoxic medicines
sec.p: One of the major toxicities associated with intermittent hypoxia is excessive erythropoiesis and elevated hemoglobin levels (Zubieta-Calleja et al., 2007). An alternative strategy to reduce tissue oxygen tension is to increase the affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen, thereby decreasing the pool of free, unbound oxygen. Drugs originally developed for sickle cell disease, including voxelotor (formerly GBT440) (Hutchaleelaha et al., 2019) and mitapivat, have been approved by the FDA based on this principle. In preclinical proof-of-concept studies, voxelotor was repurposed as a “hypoxic pill” in combination with the HIF-2α inhibitor PT2399, which suppresses hypoxia-induced erythropoiesis. This combination reduced brain tissue oxygen tension by approximately 36% in mice, an effect comparable to continuous exposure to 11% oxygen (Wang et al., 2024).

Collectively, these studies suggest that hypoxia represents a therapeutic strategy distinct from approaches that target individual molecular defects. By reducing oxygen availability, hypoxia reshapes the biochemical landscape sensed by oxygen-dependent enzymes and acts at the level of cellular state to restore epigenetic and metabolic balance in mitochondrial dysfunction and aging. Despite challenges for clinical translation, including safety and dosing, hypoxia-based interventions offer a compelling framework for reconsidering oxygen as a therapeutic variable in aging and age-associated disease.

caption.p: O₂- and α-ketoglutarate–dependent dioxygenases. Histone lysine demethylases (KDMs), prolyl hydroxylase domain protein 2 (PHD2; HIF-α prolyl hydroxylase), ten–eleven translocation enzymes (TET; 5-methylcytosine demethylases), and AlkB homolog (ALKBH) family RNA/DNA demethylases catalyze hydroxylation of methylated lysine residues, nucleic acids, or proline residues in an O₂- and α-ketoglutarate–dependent manner. These reactions require Fe(II) and reduced vitamin C as cofactors and generate hydroxylated substrates, succinate, CO₂, Fe(III), and oxidized vitamin C as products.

O2 and α-KG dependent regulation of HIF-α stability and trans-activity. Under normoxic conditions, HIF-α is hydroxylated at conserved 564th proline and 803rd asparagine residues by prolyl hydroxylase domain proteins (PHDs) and factor inhibiting HIF (FIH), respectively. These dioxygenases require molecular oxygen and α-ketoglutarate (α-KG) as co-substrates, as well as Fe(II) and reducing agents such as vitamin C for catalytic activity. Von Hippel Lindau (VHL) E3 ubiquitin ligase recognized the hydoxylated 564th proline residue to initiate ubiquitylation of HIF-α. The ubiquitinylated HIF- α is degraded by 26S proteasome. The hydroxylated 803rd asparagine residue hinders a coactivator CBP to bind its C-terminal transactivation domains. Under hypoxia, the stabilized HIF-α translocates to the nucleus and heterodimerizes with its partner HIF- β /ARNT. The HIF-α/β complex binds hypoxia-responsive elements (HREs) within promoters or enhancers of hundreds of hypoxia-regulated genes, thereby activating their transcription.

Two oxygen-dependent epigenetic regulators acting as hypoxia sensors. (A) PHD and FIH-1 (B) Histone lysine demethylases (KDMs) are activated by availabilities of their substrates oxygen and α-ketoglutarate (α-KG), as well as their cofactors Fe(II) and vitamin C. The elevated succinate, their product and reactive oxygen species (ROS), oxiding their cofactors inhibited the catalytic activities of PHD FIH and KDMs. Their activities are modulated by mitochondrial metabolism which changes the levels of oxygen, α-KG, succinate and ROS The members of the KDM4 family catalyze demethylation of methylated H3K9and H3K36. H3K9me3 is a hallmark of heterochromatin. Removal of H3K9 methylation weakens heterochromatin structure, linking oxygen-dependent KDM activity to chromatin organization.

Metabolic reactions that modulate the effective concentration of α-ketoglutarate (α-KG). Glucose is metabolized to pyruvate through glycolysis, after which pyruvate is converted to acetyl-CoA by pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) and enters the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle. Within the TCA cycle, isocitrate dehydrogenases IDH1 and IDH2 catalyze the conversion of isocitrate to α-KG. Under hypoxic conditions, glycolysis is enhanced through HIF-1α–mediated upregulation of glucose transporters and glycolytic enzymes. Concurrently, HIF-1α induces pyruvate dehydrogenase kinases (PDKs), which phosphorylate and inhibit PDH, thereby limiting the entry of pyruvate into the TCA cycle and reducing mitochondrial oxidative metabolism. Hypoxia also alters α-KG metabolism through increased expression of lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA) and malate dehydrogenases (MDH1/2), which promote the production of L-2-hydroxyglutarate (L-2HG). L-2HG acts as a competitive inhibitor of α-KG–dependent dioxygenases, effectively reducing α-KG availability for these enzymes. In parallel, glutamine uptake and glutaminolysis are upregulated under hypoxia, providing an alternative source of α-KG via conversion of glutamine to glutamate and subsequently to α-KG, thereby supporting TCA cycle intermediates despite reduced glucose-derived input.

Hypoxia limits epigenetic entropy and transcriptional noise during senescence. During oncogene-induced senescence (OIS), reductions in lamin B1 levels together with decreased levels of the heterochromatin mark H3K9me3 weaken interactions between the nuclear lamina, heterochromatin protein 1 (HP1), and H3K9me3. This destabilization facilitates detachment of heterochromatin from the nuclear periphery and contributes to loss of epigenetic constraints and increased transcriptional noise. Hypoxia maintains elevated H3K9me3 levels, thereby preserving lamina–heterochromatin interactions, limiting epigenetic information loss, and constraining transcriptional variability.
